title: The Ramayana
tagline: Rama, Sita and the long journey
description: A dedicated, stage-by-stage study of the Ramayana: the story told Kanda by Kanda, its characters and values, its many versions across India and Asia (Valmiki, Kamban, Tulsidas, Jain, Buddhist and Southeast Asian tellings), its place in festivals and the arts, and the questions readers have long debated. The epic is presented as a traditional narrative that many Hindus also hold as sacred; textual history and interpretations are clearly labelled.

structure.title: The seven Kandas of Valmiki's Ramayana
structure.intro: Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana — about 24,000 verses — is traditionally divided into seven books called Kandas. Many scholars consider the first and last Kandas to be later additions, while the tradition holds the whole text as Valmiki's. Other versions arrange or tell the story differently.

sections.name: Bala Kanda (Book of Childhood)
sections.summary: The birth of Rama and his brothers to King Dasharatha of Ayodhya; Rama and Lakshmana travel with the sage Vishvamitra; Rama strings Shiva's great bow and marries Sita of Mithila.

sections.name: Ayodhya Kanda (Book of Ayodhya)
sections.summary: Dasharatha plans to crown Rama, but Queen Kaikeyi claims two promised boons: Rama's exile for fourteen years and Bharata's crowning. Rama accepts; Sita and Lakshmana go with him. Bharata refuses to rule and places Rama's sandals on the throne.

sections.name: Aranya Kanda (Book of the Forest)
sections.summary: Life in the forest; the encounter with Shurpanakha; the golden deer; Ravana abducts Sita; the vulture Jatayu tries to save her; Rama meets Shabari.

sections.name: Kishkindha Kanda (Book of Kishkindha)
sections.summary: Rama meets Hanuman and Sugriva, helps Sugriva regain his kingdom from Vali, and the vanaras search in every direction for Sita.

sections.name: Sundara Kanda (Book of Beauty)
sections.summary: Hanuman leaps across the ocean to Lanka, finds Sita in the Ashoka grove, gives her Rama's ring, and returns with news after Lanka is set alight.

sections.name: Yuddha Kanda (Book of War)
sections.summary: The bridge to Lanka (Rama Setu); Vibhishana joins Rama; the great battle; Ravana is defeated; Sita's ordeal; the return to Ayodhya and Rama's coronation.

sections.name: Uttara Kanda (Later Book)
sections.summary: Rama's reign; Sita's exile and the birth of Lava and Kusha in Valmiki's ashram; the end of Sita's earthly life and Rama's. Many scholars see this book as a later layer, and its events are widely discussed and interpreted.

lessons.title: Who's Who in the Ramayana
objectives: Name Rama, Sita, Lakshmana, Hanuman and Ravana
Describe one quality of each character
explanation: The Ramayana is a very old story from India. It is told in many languages and in many ways, and people have loved it for a very long time.

Rama is a prince of Ayodhya, known for being kind, truthful and brave. Sita is his wife, wise and courageous. Lakshmana is Rama's loyal brother who goes everywhere with him. Hanuman is a strong and devoted helper who can leap across the sea.
Ravana is the king of Lanka, very powerful and clever, who takes Sita away. The story tells how Rama, Lakshmana and Hanuman bring Sita home.

context.text: The Ramayana is a traditional story told for over two thousand years; Valmiki is honoured as its first poet.
Many Hindus worship Rama as an avatar (form) of the god Vishnu and Hanuman as a deity of devotion and strength.

vocabulary.meaning: not giving up even when scared

story.title: The Little Squirrel
story.text: A story often told with the Ramayana says that when the monkeys were building a bridge to Lanka, a little squirrel rolled in the sand and shook it onto the bridge to help. The big monkeys laughed. But Rama gently stroked the squirrel's back and thanked it — and some say that is why squirrels have stripes. Every helper matters, big or small.

lessons.title: The Story in Four Steps
objectives: Retell the main story in four steps

explanation: First, Rama has to leave Ayodhya and live in the forest for fourteen years. Sita and Lakshmana go with him.
Next, Ravana takes Sita away to his kingdom of Lanka across the sea. Then, Hanuman leaps across the sea, finds Sita and tells her Rama is coming.
Finally, Rama, Lakshmana, Hanuman and their friends cross the sea, rescue Sita and return home to Ayodhya, where everyone welcomes them.

explanation: In many parts of India, people tell that when Rama, Sita and Lakshmana came home to Ayodhya, the people lit rows of lamps to welcome them. This is one story behind Diwali, the festival of lights.
On Diwali, families light diyas, make rangoli, share sweets and wear new clothes.
Different families and communities connect Diwali with different stories too — and all of them celebrate light, goodness and togetherness.

context.text: Linking Diwali to Rama's return is a widespread tradition, especially in north India; other communities associate Diwali with Lakshmi, Krishna, Mahavira's nirvana or Bandi Chhor Divas.

lessons.title: Bharata and the Sandals
objectives: Retell the events of the exile
Discuss why Bharata refused the throne
explanation: King Dasharatha of Ayodhya had four sons: Rama, Lakshmana, Bharata and Shatrughna. As a young man, Rama strung the great bow of Shiva in Mithila and married Sita.

When Dasharatha planned to crown Rama, Queen Kaikeyi reminded him of two promises (boons) he had once given her. She asked that Rama go to the forest for fourteen years and that her son Bharata become king. Dasharatha was heartbroken, but he had given his word. Rama accepted calmly.

Bharata was away and refused to take the throne when he returned. He went to the forest to bring Rama back. When Rama would not break his father's promise, Bharata carried Rama's sandals back and placed them on the throne, ruling only on Rama's behalf.

context.text: These events are told in Valmiki's Ayodhya Kanda and retold in many later versions.
Readers discuss Kaikeyi in different ways: some see a villain, others a mother influenced by her maid Manthara, and some versions show her later remorse.

vocabulary.meaning: the special seat of a king

examples: Bharata ruling from Nandigram with Rama's sandals on the throne.

story.title: The Sandals on the Throne
story.text: Bharata walked into the forest and fell at Rama's feet. "Come back and be king!" he begged. Rama shook his head gently: "Our father gave his word. I must keep it." Bharata thought, then asked for Rama's wooden sandals. He carried them on his head back to Ayodhya and placed them on the throne. "These will rule," he said, "until my brother returns."

lessons.title: The Golden Deer and Brave Jatayu
objectives: Retell the events of the Aranya Kanda
Discuss courage and devotion in Jatayu and Shabari
explanation: Rama, Sita and Lakshmana lived simply in the forest at Panchavati. One day, a beautiful golden deer appeared. Sita asked Rama to catch it. It was really Maricha, a demon in disguise, sent to trick them.

While Rama chased the deer and Lakshmana went to help him, Ravana came disguised as a holy man and carried Sita away in his flying chariot. The old vulture Jatayu tried bravely to stop Ravana and was badly wounded. Before he died, he told Rama which way Ravana had gone.

Searching for Sita, Rama met Shabari, an elderly woman who had waited many years to see him. In a much-loved telling, she tasted each berry to offer him only the sweet ones, and Rama accepted them happily, valuing her devotion.

context.text: The golden deer and Jatayu appear in Valmiki's Aranya Kanda; the detail of Shabari tasting the berries is popular in later devotional retellings.
For many devotees, Shabari's story teaches that sincere devotion matters more than status or ritual.

vocabulary.meaning: clothes or a shape that hides who you really are

story.title: Jatayu's Brave Flight
story.text: High above the forest, old Jatayu saw Ravana's chariot carrying Sita away. Though he was old and tired, he spread his great wings and flew at the chariot. He fought with all his strength until he was badly hurt. When Rama found him, Jatayu whispered which way Ravana had gone. "He gave everything to help," Rama said, honouring him.

lessons.title: Hanuman and Sugriva
objectives: Retell how Rama met Hanuman and Sugriva
Discuss friendship and keeping promises
explanation: Searching for Sita, Rama and Lakshmana reached Kishkindha, the kingdom of the vanaras (monkey-people). There they met Hanuman, the wise and powerful minister of Sugriva.

Sugriva had been driven from his kingdom by his brother Vali. Rama and Sugriva became friends and made promises: Rama would help Sugriva, and Sugriva would help find Sita. After Rama helped Sugriva regain his kingdom, the vanaras searched north, south, east and west.
The southern search party, with Hanuman, Angada and the wise bear Jambavan, learned from the vulture Sampati (Jatayu's brother) that Sita was in Lanka across the sea.

context.text: Kishkindha is traditionally associated with the region around Hampi in Karnataka.
Rama's role in the conflict between Vali and Sugriva is one of the episodes readers and commentators have long debated.

lessons.title: Hanuman Finds Sita
objectives: Retell the events of the Sundara Kanda
Describe Hanuman's qualities
explanation: Hanuman leaped across the ocean to Lanka. Making himself tiny, he searched Ravana's golden city at night until he found Sita in the Ashoka grove, guarded and sad but steadfast.

He gave her Rama's ring as proof, and she gave him her hair jewel (chudamani) to take back to Rama. Hanuman was then captured; Ravana's men set his tail on fire, but he escaped and leapt across the rooftops, setting Lanka ablaze before returning.
The Sundara Kanda — the "beautiful book" — is especially loved; many devotees read or recite it, and Hanuman is admired for courage, intelligence, humility and devotion.

context.text: Many Hindus recite the Sundara Kanda or the Hanuman Chalisa (by Tulsidas) for strength and protection.
Details such as Hanuman changing size come from the traditional narrative.

lessons.title: Vibhishana's Choice
objectives: Retell the key events of the Yuddha Kanda
Discuss Vibhishana's decision to choose what is right
explanation: Rama's army reached the southern sea. The vanaras, led by the engineers Nala and Nila, built a bridge of stones across to Lanka, known as the Rama Setu.

Ravana's brother Vibhishana advised him to return Sita and make peace. When Ravana angrily refused, Vibhishana left Lanka and joined Rama, who welcomed him. Choosing what is right over loyalty to family was very hard.

In the great battle, many heroes fought. Finally Rama defeated Ravana. Sita was reunited with Rama, and they returned to Ayodhya, where Rama was crowned. Rama's reign is remembered in tradition as "Ram Rajya", an ideal of just rule.

context.text: The bridge, the battle and the coronation are central episodes of the Yuddha Kanda.
A natural chain of limestone shoals between India and Sri Lanka is known as Adam's Bridge or Rama Setu; geologists study it as a natural formation, while many people associate it with the epic.
The episode of Sita's fire ordeal (agni pariksha) after the battle is told differently in different versions and is widely discussed and questioned by readers.

examples: Stones floating to form the bridge in the story.

lessons.title: Heroes and Villains Are Complicated
objectives: Analyse characters using evidence from the story
Recognise that even "villains" are complex
explanation: Rama is called "maryada purushottam" — the ideal man who follows dharma. Yet readers ask hard questions about some of his choices, such as the killing of Vali from hiding and his treatment of Sita.

Sita is often seen as an ideal of devotion, but she is also strong and decisive: she insists on going to the forest, resists Ravana's threats for months, and in some versions speaks powerfully for herself.

Ravana is a great scholar, a devotee of Shiva and a mighty king, yet his pride and desire bring ruin. Kumbhakarna, his brother, tells him he is wrong but fights for him anyway. Lesser-known characters like Urmila, Lakshmana's wife who stays behind, have inspired new retellings.

context.text: Many Hindus revere Rama as maryada purushottam and an avatar of Vishnu.
Discussing characters' choices is a long-standing part of the tradition itself; commentators, poets and modern writers have offered many interpretations.

vocabulary.meaning: the ideal person who upholds dharma

examples: Ravana composing the Shiva Tandava Stotram in tradition.

story.title: Kumbhakarna Awakens
story.text: Woken from his long sleep for the war, the giant Kumbhakarna listened to his brother. "You were wrong to take Sita," he said plainly. "But you are my brother, and Lanka is my home." Then he went out to fight. Students reading his story often argue: was he loyal, or was he wrong to fight for a cause he knew was unjust?

lessons.title: When Duties Clash
objectives: Explain dharma as right action that can conflict
Analyse a dilemma from the Ramayana from several perspectives
explanation: Dharma means right action, duty and moral order. In the Ramayana, characters often face situations where duties clash.

Dasharatha must choose between his promise to Kaikeyi and his love for Rama. Vibhishana chooses between loyalty to his brother and what he believes is right. In the Uttara Kanda, Rama as king exiles Sita because of public gossip — a choice between kingly duty as he saw it and personal love that many readers find deeply troubling.

There are no easy answers. Different traditions, poets and readers have responded differently — Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas does not include Sita's exile in its main narrative; Bhavabhuti's play Uttararamacharita gives it a reconciling ending.

context.text: Sita's exile is one of the most discussed episodes in the tradition; responses range from defending Rama's royal duty to critiquing the treatment of Sita.
Bhavabhuti's Sanskrit play Uttararamacharita (8th century CE) reimagines the ending with Rama and Sita reunited.

vocabulary.meaning: right action, duty and moral order
a choice between conflicting duties or values

examples: Dasharatha's promise and love in conflict.

lessons.title: Lessons for Today
objectives: Connect values in the Ramayana to everyday life
Express personal reflections respectfully
explanation: Many people find values in the Ramayana that matter today: keeping promises, loyalty between siblings (Rama and his brothers), friendship across differences (Rama with Sugriva, Vibhishana and Jatayu), and respect for all creatures, from the squirrel to the vulture.
The story also invites questions about fairness, gender roles and leadership, which modern readers discuss openly.
People of all backgrounds can learn from the Ramayana as literature, while many Hindus also hold it as sacred. Both ways of reading can be respectful.

context.text: For many devotees, the Ramayana is a sacred text and Rama is worshipped.
Readers of different backgrounds draw different lessons; modern retellings, such as those centring Sita's perspective, add new voices.

lessons.title: One Story, Many Tellings
objectives: Describe major versions of the Ramayana
Compare how versions differ and why
explanation: Valmiki's Sanskrit Ramayana is the earliest full version. Scholars estimate it was composed in stages, roughly between the 5th century BCE and the early centuries CE, though dates are debated.

Later poets retold it in their own languages and devotional styles: Kamban's Tamil Ramavataram (12th century), Krittivasa's Bengali version (15th century), Tulsidas's Awadhi Ramcharitmanas (16th century), and many more in Telugu, Kannada, Marathi, Malayalam and other languages.

Jain versions (such as Vimalasuri's Paumachariya) and Buddhist Jataka stories tell it differently — for example, in some Jain tellings, Lakshmana, not Rama, kills Ravana. Folk, women's and tribal songs add still more perspectives.

context.text: Textual scholars date layers of Valmiki's Ramayana using linguistic and historical analysis; estimates range widely.
Within many Hindu traditions, Valmiki's Ramayana and Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas are revered as sacred.
Scholar A. K. Ramanujan's essay "Three Hundred Ramayanas" argued that there are many Ramayanas, each with its own meaning — a view some have embraced and others contested.

story.title: The Poet in Varanasi

Some scholars of his time objected. But his Ramcharitmanas became one of the most beloved books in north India, recited and sung in millions of homes.

lessons.title: Rama Travels Abroad
objectives: Describe Ramayana traditions in Southeast Asia
Explain how the story spread and adapted
explanation: Through trade, travel and cultural exchange over many centuries, the Ramayana reached Southeast Asia.

In Thailand, it became the Ramakien, and the city of Ayutthaya was named after Ayodhya. In Cambodia, the Reamker is performed in classical dance, and Angkor Wat's walls show Ramayana scenes. In Indonesia, the Old Javanese Kakawin Ramayana inspired wayang shadow puppetry and dance at Prambanan temple — in a Muslim-majority country, the story remains a shared cultural treasure.
Each culture adapted the story: Hanuman, for example, has more adventures and romance in the Ramakien.

context.text: Ramayana reliefs at Prambanan (9th century) and Angkor Wat (12th century) are physical evidence of the epic's spread.
Southeast Asian Ramayanas developed their own traditions, characters and episodes.

The audience — Muslim, Hindu and others — laughed and gasped at the familiar story. "It's our story too," a grandfather said.

lessons.title: From Ramlila to Animation
objectives: Describe artistic traditions based on the Ramayana

explanation: Ramlila — a dramatic performance of the Ramayana, often over many nights around Dussehra — is performed across north India. The Ramlila of Ramnagar near Varanasi lasts about a month. UNESCO recognises Ramlila as intangible cultural heritage.
Classical and folk forms like Kathakali (Kerala), Yakshagana (Karnataka) and Chhau (eastern India) dramatise episodes. Rajput and Pahari miniature paintings illustrated the epic in vivid detail.

Modern media continue the tradition: the 1987–88 TV serial Ramayan by Ramanand Sagar was watched by enormous audiences, and comics, animated films and novels keep retelling it, sometimes from new perspectives.

context.text: UNESCO inscribed "Ramlila, the traditional performance of the Ramayana" on its intangible heritage list in 2008.
Many communities perform Ramlila as an act of devotion as well as entertainment.

lessons.title: The First Poem
objectives: Explain why Valmiki's Ramayana is called the adikavya
Analyse its literary features such as metre, rasa and frame narrative
prerequisites: Knows versions and the story in depth
explanation: Tradition calls Valmiki the adikavi (first poet) and his Ramayana the adikavya (first poem) of Sanskrit literature. A famous story tells that Valmiki saw a hunter shoot one of a pair of krauncha birds; his grief (shoka) spontaneously became a verse in the shloka metre.
The shloka has four quarters of eight syllables. The dominant rasa (aesthetic mood) of the Ramayana is often said to be karuna — compassion or pathos — though heroism (vira) is also central.
The epic uses a frame: Valmiki teaches the poem to Lava and Kusha, Rama's sons, who sing it in Rama's own court. This layered storytelling invites reflection on how stories are transmitted.

context.text: The krauncha bird story and Valmiki's status as adikavi come from the tradition, including the Bala Kanda itself.
Literary critics, including classical theorists like Anandavardhana, discussed karuna as the Ramayana's principal rasa.

story.title: The Birth of a Verse

lessons.title: Evidence, Faith and Respect
objectives: Distinguish historical, textual and faith-based questions about the Ramayana
Engage with contemporary interpretations respectfully
explanation: Different questions need different methods. Textual scholars ask when and how texts were composed, using manuscripts and language. Archaeologists look for physical evidence of places and periods. These questions are answered with evidence and remain open to revision.

For many Hindus, the Ramayana is sacred and Rama is a deity; questions of faith are not settled by archaeology, and belief deserves respect. At the same time, presenting traditional narratives as documented history without evidence, or using them to demean others, misuses both history and faith.

Contemporary interpretations include feminist readings centred on Sita (such as in Chitra Banerjee Divakaruni's "The Forest of Enchantments"), Dalit and regional perspectives, and debates in public life. Thoughtful readers listen to multiple voices with care.

context.text: Textual criticism uses manuscripts; the Baroda Critical Edition of Valmiki's Ramayana (1960–75) compared many manuscripts to reconstruct an early text.
For many Hindus, Rama is a divine avatar, and the Ramayana is a sacred guide to dharma.
Modern scholarship, devotional commentary and literary retellings offer different and sometimes conflicting readings.

The teacher said, "Each of you asked a different kind of question. Respecting that difference is how we learn together."
